in_context.text: This verse finishes the greeting of Paul's letter to Philemon. Besides Philemon, Paul greets Apphia, Archippus, and the whole church that met in Philemon's house. So a personal appeal about Onesimus is also read in front of the gathered believers.

speaker.text: Paul, writing as "a prisoner of Jesus Christ," together with Timothy.

audience.text: Philemon is the main addressee. Apphia, Archippus, and the church meeting in Philemon's house are named with him.

what.text: Paul names Apphia as a beloved believer and Archippus as a "fellowsoldier," a partner in Christian service. He includes the house church in the greeting. The text does not say how Apphia or Archippus were related to Philemon.

events.text: The greeting opens a letter Paul sent while in prison, before Onesimus returned to Philemon.

written.text: Traditional: about AD 60-62, from prison in Rome, at the same time as Colossians. Scholarly: nearly all accept Paul wrote it, but some place the imprisonment at Ephesus (about AD 54-55) or Caesarea (about AD 57-59).

where.text: The church met in a home, "thy house" (Philemon's). The letter does not name the town, but Colossae is indicated because Colossians also sends a message to Archippus.

purpose.text: By greeting the whole house church, Paul places his request about Onesimus before the community. Philemon's response to receiving Onesimus as "a brother beloved" becomes a matter of shared faith and love.

big_picture.text: Early believers often gathered in homes. Paul greets other house churches the same way, such as those of Priscilla and Aquila and of Nymphas.

for_readers.text: Faith is lived among fellow believers, not alone. Paul treats ordinary church members as family and fellow workers in the Lord.

why_it_matters.text: The word here is glossed "our sister." It is used of a fellow member of the Christian community, as with Phoebe in Romans 16:1. Apphia is greeted as family in the faith.

It means a fellow soldier and is used figuratively of fellowship in Christian service. The only other use is for Epaphroditus in Philippians 2:25. Paul elsewhere pictures the believer as "a good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2 Timothy 2:3).
The word means an assembly. In the New Testament it is used especially of a company of Christians. Here it means the people gathered, not a building.
The word means a house or dwelling, a home. The church met in an ordinary home, as other churches did.

takeaway.text: Paul's private appeal is set within a church family meeting in a home. Fellow believers are sisters, brothers, and fellow soldiers in the Lord's service.
